headings.title: Introduction to Data Presentation and Pie Charts
headings.content: Data presentation turns raw healthcare numbers into clear pictures. In Nigerian nursing research and hospital audits, we collect plenty of figures—such as patient admission diagnoses, vaccine uptake rates, or ward staffing ratios. Showing these numbers in tables alone can be tiring for readers. A pie chart offers a visual shortcut by dividing a single round circle into slices. Each slice stands for a specific category, making the whole circle equal to one hundred percent of the data set. Nurses use this tool during ward presentations and quality improvement meetings to show proportions at a single glance.

headings.title: Core Concepts: Proportions and Percentages in Nursing Data
headings.content: Every pie chart relies on parts making up a whole. When recording infection control data across four clinical wards, the total number of patients across all wards represents the whole, or one hundred percent. A single ward's patient count forms a fraction of that total. To put this on a chart, we convert that fraction into a percentage. For instance, if 20 out of 100 children in a paediatric unit suffer from severe dehydration, that subgroup makes up 20 percent of the total patient group. Grasping this part-to-whole relationship is necessary before drawing any reliable healthcare graph.

headings.title: When to Use a Pie Chart in Healthcare Research
headings.content:
Pie charts are not meant for every type of nursing research data. They work best when displaying categorical data divided into a small number of distinct groups—ideally six or fewer. 

- **Good fit**: Showing the percentage of patients presenting with various blood groups in an antenatal clinic.
- **Good fit**: Illustrating the primary sources of funding for a community health outreach program.
- **Poor fit**: Displaying patient blood pressure readings taken over twelve consecutive hours.

Trying to pack too many categories into one circle creates thin, unreadable slices. For tracking trends over time, a line graph remains the superior choice.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Calculation of Degrees and Percentages
headings.content:
Drawing an accurate pie chart requires translating percentages into geometric degrees because a circle measures 360 degrees in total. 

1. **Find the total**: Add up all individual frequencies to get the grand total.
2. **Calculate the percentage**: Divide each category value by the total and multiply by 100.
3. **Calculate the degrees**: Multiply the decimal fraction of the category by 360 degrees.

For example, if 50 patients out of 200 have malaria, the fraction is 0.25. Multiply 0.25 by 360 degrees to get 90 degrees for that specific slice.

headings.title: Constructing and Interpreting a Pie Chart
headings.content: Constructing a clear chart demands careful manual work or proper software settings. Start by drawing a clean circle using a pair of compasses. Use a protractor to measure each calculated degree outward from the center point, drawing straight lines to the edge. Label each slice clearly with the category name and its percentage value rather than the raw number alone. When reading a completed chart, look for the largest slice to quickly spot the most common finding, such as the leading cause of ward admissions during a rainy season.

headings.title: Advantages and Limitations of Pie Charts
headings.content:
| Advantages | Limitations |
| :--- | :--- |
| Simple visual appeal for lay audiences | Difficult to compare two similar-sized slices |
| Clearly shows part-to-whole relationships | Fails to show changes over time |
| Easy to create in basic software | Unusable with large numbers of categories |

While patients and hospital administrators appreciate the simplicity of a pie chart during briefings, researchers often prefer bar charts. The human eye struggles to accurately judge slight differences in slice angles, making precise data comparison tough.

headings.title: Common Pitfalls and Best Practices in Nursing Statistics
headings.content: Errors in data presentation undermine the credibility of nursing audits. A frequent mistake is failing to ensure that all slice percentages add up to exactly one hundred percent due to rounding errors. Another pitfall is 3D styling, which distorts visual perception by making slices in the front look deceptively larger than slices in the back. Always keep charts simple, flat, and clearly labeled. Ensure the chart title states the exact setting and time frame so readers know precisely what population the data describes.
